_doc: Authored T-0478 findings for the fourth 75-person pass. Omitted cohort members receive documented no-corroboration outcomes; regional and same-name candidates remain unasserted resident facts.
default_summary: No reliable record found in the reviewed repository reference corpus, contemporary newspaper searches, institutional/local histories, directories and regional genealogy/index searches could be tied to this person by more than the recorded name. This is a documented no-find, not evidence that the person did not exist.

handy_major.summary: Cook County/early-Chicago history independently places Major Handy in the 1833 river-improvement work. The exact name and distinctive public-work role strengthen the resident identity without proving a July 1835 dwelling.

mason_matthias.summary: Early Cook County history identifies Matthias/Mathias Mason opening a Chicago blacksmith shop in fall 1833. The uncommon name, trade, place and date independently support the profile; spelling variants are retained as variants rather than separate people.

maxwell_philip.summary: Chicago medical history gives Philip Maxwell's full birth data and places him as Fort Dearborn's last surgeon from 1833 through the fort's final 1836 abandonment. This strongly corroborates his scene-period Chicago role.

mckee_david.summary: Early Chicago histories independently identify David McKee as the government/agency blacksmith near the foot of State Street. The occupation and institutional role are distinctive enough to corroborate the resident record, while the exact July 1835 workplace continuity is not extended beyond the sources.

meeker_joseph.summary: The First Presbyterian history says Joseph Meeker came to Chicago early in 1833, joined the church September 8, 1833, served as Sunday-school librarian March 16, 1835, and built the congregation's first meeting house. These dated institutional roles strongly corroborate his Chicago presence close to the scene date.

miller_john.summary: Retrospective Chicago histories independently identify John Miller with the settlement's first tannery, built near the North Branch/forks in 1831. The exact name, unusual trade and site corroborate the profile without inventing a July 1835 residence.

mulford_e_h.summary: The current E. H. Mulford watchmaker record conflicts with stronger same-period evidence: the project's July/August 1835 Chicago Democrat corpus prints J. H. Mulford in watches and jewelry, while later directories distinguish Major E. H. Mulford from James H. and Edward H. Jr. The household may conflate members of the Mulford family, so no automatic rename or relationship is asserted.

candidates.name: James H. Mulford, Chicago jeweler/watch dealer
candidates.basis: Near-contemporary July/August 1835 newspaper text prints J. H. Mulford in the watch/jewelry trade, matching the distinctive occupation.
conflicts: Existing Andreas-derived record says E. H. Mulford and arrival 1833; later sources distinguish multiple Mulford men in the jewelry business.

murphy_john.summary: Cook County history reports John and Harriet Murphy taking charge of Mark Beaubien's new Exchange Coffee House in August 1834 and remaining until 1836. The named spouse, hotel and bounded chronology strongly corroborate the household across the scene date.

norton_nelson_r.summary: Early Chicago history preserves Nelson R. Norton's own chronology: arrival November 16, 1833, construction of the Dearborn Street drawbridge beginning March 1834 and completion around June. Exact name plus the distinctive shipwright/bridge role corroborate the person.

pierce_asahel.summary: Early Chicago history identifies Asahel Pierce as an October 1833 arrival and blacksmith/agricultural-implement maker. The uncommon name and distinctive trade provide independent corroboration, but no unsupported July 1835 roof is added.

porthier_joseph.summary: Pioneer History of Milwaukee supplies a materially tighter migration chronology than the existing record: Joseph Porthier left Chicago with Horace Chase on February 27, 1835, briefly returned to Chicago for means, then left again March 21 and reached Milwaukee March 23. This places his removal before the July 1 scene date.

population_updates.reason: Dated February–March 1835 migration chronology places Porthier in Milwaukee before July 1.

pruyne_peter.summary: Medical/pharmaceutical histories independently identify Peter Pruyne and Edmund Stoughton Kimberly as operators of Chicago's second drug store from early 1833. The business partnership strengthens Pruyne's profile but does not by itself establish a dwelling.

kimberly_edmund_s.summary: Chicago medical history expands Edmund Stoughton Kimberly with an exact birth date of April 7, 1803, medical education, 1829 marriage, 1832 move to Chicago, 1833 town-trustee service and 1834 cholera-hospital authorization. These are independent discriminators beyond surname or household association.

sproat_grenville.summary: Early education histories identify Granville T. Sproat opening an English and Classical School in Chicago in fall 1833 and Sarah L. Warren assisting him in March 1834. The source's Granville spelling is retained as a variant against the repository's Grenville spelling rather than silently normalized.

st_cyr_john_mary.summary: Catholic institutional history independently places John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr's appointment to Chicago in 1833, first Mass and first church construction, with recall in 1837. The bounded ministry strongly corroborates his presence during 1835.

steele_ashbel.summary: Cook County histories place Ashbel Steele in the early Chicago/Cook County civic record and identify him as county coroner in the 1835 period. This supports continued local presence while stopping short of assigning an unsourced town dwelling.

sweet_alanson.summary: Milwaukee histories identify Alanson Sweet as an early Chicago stone mason who moved to Milwaukee in 1835. The migration is real and important, but the reviewed passage does not supply a sufficiently safe departure day to convert July 1 presence from uncertain to absent.

thomas_frederick.summary: The Encyclopedia of Chicago independently identifies Frederick Thomas as Chicago's first barber-surgeon and a retail druggist in the 1830s, corroborating the unusual combined occupation. The project newspaper corpus remains the stronger path for exact 1835 advertising/address detail.

walters_william.summary: Andreas-derived Wolf Point history gives William Walters as proprietor of the Wolf Point Tavern from 1833 through 1836. That strongly supports scene-period continuity, but because it is a retrospective year range rather than a July 1 instrument the household's cautious presence flag is not silently upgraded here.

watkins_john.summary: Cook County education history specifically says John Watkins taught a successful school in Chicago in 1835; another early account says he was again on the North Side that year. This independently corroborates occupation and scene-year presence.

kinzie_james.summary: Early Chicago civic/business histories distinguish James Kinzie from the other Kinzie men and connect him with Wolf Point, auctioneering and early town affairs. The pass keeps those identities separate rather than treating the surname as a household merge rule.

kinzie_robert_a.summary: Published Cook County biography states Robert A. Kinzie remained mostly in Chicago from 1825 to 1840, built a frame store in 1832 and became a member of Kinzie, Davis & Hyde in 1835. Exact name, family context, business and year strongly corroborate the profile.

paine_seth.summary: Andreas's Seth Paine biography gives an exact uncommon name and a direct 1834 migration from Montpelier, Vermont to Chicago. In combination with the 1835 postal entry, this is sufficient to treat the postal name as strongly corroborated while not importing Paine's much later banking or abolitionist activity into the 1835 scene.

titcomb_timothy.summary: Wheeling history places Timothy Titcomb on Section 13 among 1834 settlers. The exact uncommon name and Cook County chronology make a strong candidate for the postal entry, but the source places him in Wheeling and supplies no direct Chicago-letter bridge.

candidates.name: Timothy Titcomb of Wheeling Township
candidates.basis: Exact uncommon name, Cook County and 1834 settlement chronology.
conflicts: Hinterland residence; no record explicitly links this man to the Chicago post-office item.

ward_hanibal.summary: Will County history places Hannibal Ward among a western-New-York colony making claims in the DuPage River valley in 1833. The exact uncommon name and regional chronology are useful, but the outlying residence prevents promotion to a Chicago identity without a postal bridge.

candidates.name: Hannibal Ward of the DuPage River valley
candidates.basis: Exact uncommon name and documented 1833 northeastern Illinois settlement.
conflicts: Documented outside Chicago; no source ties him directly to this letter.

white_edson.summary: Will County history lists Edson White among Joliet's 1835 arrivals. Exact uncommon name and same-year regional presence make a plausible postal candidate, but Joliet is competing geography and the record does not identify him as the Chicago addressee.

candidates.name: Edson White of Joliet
candidates.basis: Exact uncommon name and 1835 northeastern Illinois chronology.
conflicts: Joliet residence; no direct Chicago-post-office linkage.
